children: Democrats are keen to investigate once they take over control of the House and Senate in January whether President Trump's "most favored nations" drug pricing deals with many of the top pharmaceutical industry actually translate into real savings for consumers and the government.

Sen. Ron Wyden (Ore.), currently the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee and a long-time thorn in Trump's side, earlier this year sought information from drugmakers on the deals they made with the government. When he becomes chair of that committee in January, he will have subpoena power, and recently said that pharma execs "that price gouge while enjoying Trump's hand-delivered windfalls" will answer to the committee,

Shortly before Election Day, House Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Rep. Frank Pallone (N.J.) asked the GAO to review TrumpRx, the website set up by the administration as a portal for consumers to obtain cheaper drugs.

While the White House has stated that "most favored nation" drug pricing will save $600 billion over the next 10 years, there are questions over the real savings. The government already generates cost savings through existing Medicaid drug pricing deals, and many high-cost medicines in Medicare Part D have come down due to provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act that subject certain therapies to price negotiations. Also, the agreements signed with drugmakers end when Trump leaves office in January 2029.
This week, Pallone sent a letter to colleagues asking that more drugs be subject to the IRA provisions,

title: Democratic lawmakers seen probing Trump drug pricing deals come January
